scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Matins Chants in Ukrainian Irmologia of the 17th–18th Centuries
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. ### and June 29: The Holy Preeminent Apostles Peter and Paul

These two Feasts, as also the Beheading of the Precious Head of the Forerunner, have the general Typikon of a Saint with Vigil; nevertheless they surpass a Saint with Vigil in the following points:
1. At Matins, before their Canon, the Canon of the Theotokos is not taken, but only their two Canons for 14: the Heirmos of the 1st Canon twice, then the Troparia of both Canons for 12, that is, 6 of the one, and 6 of the other.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part3_menaion.md` (L3131–L3135): ### August 6: The Transfiguration of Our Lord All is according to the general Typikon of a Dominical Feast; only after the Prayer behind the Ambon[^463], as the Slavonic Typika have, or after the Dismissal of the Divine Liturgy, as the Trebnik of Peremyshl has, the Priest blesses on the Tetrapod the first-fruits of grapes (among us, however, since there are no grapes, the first-fruits of apples and other fruits) with the single prayer set down in the Menaion, or with the three prayers set down in our Trebnik[^464], with censing and the sprinkling of the same with holy water at the conclusion. > **Note:** If this blessing takes place after the Prayer behind the Ambon, we deem that there is no need to recite beforehand the Usual Beginning and the Trisagion and the rest with the **"Our Father"** (*Отче нашъ*), and Psalm 66, and the Troparion and Kontakion of the Feast[^465], but immediately **"Let us pray to the Lord"** (*Господу помолимся*), and the Prayer; for the Menaion indicates only the Prayer.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### August 6: The Transfiguration of Our Lord

All is according to the general Typikon of a Dominical Feast; only after the Prayer behind the Ambon[^463], as the Slavonic Typika have, or after the Dismissal of the Divine Liturgy, as the Trebnik of Peremyshl has, the Priest blesses on the Tetrapod the first-fruits of grapes (among us, however, since there are no grapes, the first-fruits of apples and other fruits) with the single prayer set down in the Menaion, or with the three prayers set down in our Trebnik[^464], with censing and the sprinkling of the same with holy water at the conclusion.

> **Note:** If this blessing takes place after the Prayer behind the Ambon, we deem that there is no need to recite beforehand the Usual Beginning and the Trisagion and the rest with the **"Our Father"** (*Отче нашъ*), and Psalm 66, and the Troparion and Kontakion of the Feast[^465], but immediately **"Let us pray to the Lord"** (*Господу помолимся*), and the Prayer; for the Menaion indicates only the Prayer.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Matins Chants in Ukrainian Irmologia of the 17th–18th Centuries
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### August 6: The Transfiguration of Our Lord

All is according to the general Typikon of a Dominical Feast; only after the Prayer behind the Ambon[^463], as the Slavonic Typika have, or after the Dismissal of the Divine Liturgy, as the Trebnik of Peremyshl has, the Priest blesses on the Tetrapod the first-fruits of grapes (among us, however, since there are no grapes, the first-fruits of apples and other fruits) with the single prayer set down in the Menaion, or with the three prayers set down in our Trebnik[^464], with censing and the sprinkling of the same with holy water at the conclusion.

> **Note:** If this blessing takes place after the Prayer behind the Ambon, we deem that there is no need to recite beforehand the Usual Beginning and the Trisagion and the rest with the **"Our Father"** (*Отче нашъ*), and Psalm 66, and the Troparion and Kontakion of the Feast[^465], but immediately **"Let us pray to the Lord"** (*Господу помолимся*), and the Prayer; for the Menaion indicates only the Prayer.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. ### August 15: The Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos

All is according to the general Typikon of Marian Feasts; only, if it is the custom anywhere, then after the Prayer behind the Ambon, or after the Dismissal of the Divine Liturgy, occurs the blessing of herbs, according to the Typikon set forth above for the blessing of fruits on August 6 here preceding.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. All is according to the general Typikon of Marian Feasts; only, if it is the custom anywhere, then after the Prayer behind the Ambon, or after the Dismissal of the Divine Liturgy, occurs the blessing of herbs, according to the Typikon set forth above for the blessing of fruits on August 6 here preceding.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

All these are performed as follows, and before all else the Preparation of the Precious Cross.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. The Exaltation takes place at the Tetrapod after the Great Doxology; the Veneration, however, immediately after the Exaltation, and likewise after every Divine Service celebrated in the Church even unto the Apodosis of the Feast (September 21). All these are performed as follows, and before all else the Preparation of the Precious Cross.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.
scholarly_summaries.verbatim_source: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: The monumental First Tone Dogmatikon praising the heavenly gate and song of the bodiless powers.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. pillar_1_significance.why_featured_assessment: Dogmatic exposition of the burning bush and the transition from the shadow of the law to grace.
pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Saturday Great Vespers: Tone 2 Vesperal Entrance Theotokion as a scored Dogmatikon / Theotokion (Tone 2). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: Dogmatic exposition of the burning bush and the transition from the shadow of the law to grace.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Saturday Great Vespers: Tone 3 Vesperal Entrance Theotokion as a scored Dogmatikon / Theotokion (Tone 3). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: Theology of the two natures of Christ united without confusion or division.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum.
