pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Saturday Great Vespers: Tone 4 Vesperal Entrance Theotokion as a scored Dogmatikon / Theotokion (Tone 4). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: Cites David the ancestor of God prophesying the Queen standing at the right hand of Christ.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: The celebrated Sixth Tone Dogmatikon praising the Mother of the Only-begotten Son Who became man for our salvation.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. In this context, Vespers chants are an important continuous link in Ukrainian sacred art, which requires

Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: Grave Tone theological confession of the Virgin Mother remaining untouched by mortal passion.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil

#### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing

"The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. pillar_1_significance.why_featured_assessment: The final majestic Eighth Tone Dogmatikon declaring that the Heavenly King appeared on earth and dwelt among men.
pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Saturday Great Vespers: Tone 8 Vesperal Entrance Theotokion as a scored Dogmatikon / Theotokion (Tone 8). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. John of Damascus (8th-c. Mar Saba Hagiopolite school). Theological & Musical Significance: The final majestic Eighth Tone Dogmatikon declaring that the Heavenly King appeared on earth and dwelt among men.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part1_general_order.md` (L14–L18): ### Order of Great Vespers at an All-Night Vigil #### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing "The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

#### 1. Vesting in the Sacred Vestments, and Censing

"The candles upon the High Altar being lighted, and two censers being prepared if there are two Deacons, but if not, then only one: the Priest, having blessed with his hand arranged in the manner of the Liturgical blessing the Epitrakhelion, and having kissed it where it has a cross, vests himself in it;[^4] and the Deacons vest in Dalmatics [Stikharia] with the Orarion, having kissed them first. And all three go forth, one after another—first the second Deacon, then the first, and last the Priest—from the Diakonikon before the steps of the Altar; and the second Deacon standing on the left side, the first on the right side of the Priest, with the Priest in their midst: all three bow profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries; and turning together toward the Holy Doors, the Priest and the second Deacon by their right side, and the first Deacon by his left, open them. And turning again toward the Altar with the same semicircle movement, the Deacons take the censers; and the Priest, taking the spoon with his right hand, places incense first into the censer of the first Deacon, then into the censer of the second Deacon. And when the Deacons say: **\"Bless, Master, the incense,\"** the Priest blesses both censers separately in the form of a cross, saying together the short prayer: **\"Incense we offer unto Thee,\"** found in the *Sluzhebnik* at the end of the Proskomedia. At other censings, in place of this, he says only: **\"Blessed is our God, always, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages.\"** Then, while the Priest waits in the same place, and only in cathedral churches, whether secular or monastic, the second Deacon having proclaimed: **\"Command!\"**[^5] and all having stood up, the Deacons cense—always with three movements of the censer—first the Holy Table on its four sides, that is, first from the front both together, and they bow toward the Holy Mysteries; then stepping, the first Deacon to the right side and the second Deacon to the left, they cense it from there; then its rear side (and the Icon, if there is one behind the Holy Table) both together; and the Priest from the front corners of the Altar both together. And thus they go forth, each by his own door, before the Royal Doors; and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn toward the sovereign icons of the Iconostas, each censing them from his own side; then they process with the smoking censers around the temple, each on his own side, censing at the same time also the icons of the side altars, if there be any; and having thus returned down the center of the temple from the great church doors before the Royal Doors, and having bowed profoundly toward the Holy Mysteries, they turn—the right Deacon by his left side, and the left Deacon by his right side—to the west, and each censes from his own side: first the Kliros, if it is a cathedral church, then the Choirs, and finally both together cense the people."

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Musical Features of Vesperal Dogmatika in the Kyivan-Galician Tradition
scholarly_summaries.corpus_ref: Kyivan Musicology/Academics/Wing_B_Translations_Portal/24 Moiseiev - Dogmatikas Musical Features (Bachelor Thesis)/2_Translation.md#L60
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The relevance of the present study is conditioned by the insufficient scholarly attention devoted to the genres of Ukrainian church music. Dogmatikas, stichera, canons, and other genres must today be introduced into the academic domain, particularly that of performance practice. For the chants of sacred monody play a vital role in understanding the Ukrainian musical tradition, which throughout the entirety of its existence has been and remains closely bound to professional church music, flourishing on Ukrainian lands since the time of Christianization. Therefore, the elucidation of the ancient sung texts of the dogmatikas in both monodic and choral traditions is intended to underscore their distinctiveness and uniqueness within the broader European context and must continue to engage the interest of composers and performers alike, so as to revive especially the musical culture of the 17th century, which was subjected to prohibitions over the course of three hundred years under Muscovite subjugation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Octoechos Genres Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In the early modern Ukrainian church-music tradition (16th–18th centuries), the Octoechos underwent significant generic and structural evolution. The primary vehicle of this transformation was the Ukrainian staff-notated Heirmologion, which synthesized the essential chants of disparate liturgical books into a single, comprehensive singer's manual.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum.
